name: Qfplib-M0-full (Cortex-M0 floating-point library)
baseline: GCC soft-float library (libgcc) float and double routines on ARM Cortex-M0
workload: Average cycle counts per call for single- and double-precision add, sub, mul, div, sqrt, sin, cos, tan, atan2, exp and ln on an NXP LPC11U68 (Cortex-M0, single-cycle flash), non-exceptional arguments, calling overhead included.
claimed_speedup: Cycles Qfplib vs GCC library: fadd 76 vs 102, fmul 62 vs 166, fdiv 83 vs 475, fsqrt 67 vs 460, fsin 584 vs 3300, fexp 261 vs 1930, dmul 163 vs 377, ddiv 200 vs 1190, dsqrt 174 vs 1305, dln 464 vs 4375. README also says the double-precision Qfplib routines are faster than the GCC single-precision ones in every case.
stars_or_usage: 17 stars, 8 forks (RT-Thread packaging of the upstream Qfplib; README links quinapalus.com/qfplib.html for the original)
tradeoffs: ARMv6-M (Cortex-M0) only, GNU assembler source (qfplib-m0-full_gcc.S) with a C header. Under 6 kbyte of program memory, no static storage, no recursion. Not drop-in IEEE-exact for exceptional arguments: README says the cycle figures are for non-exceptional arguments. GPLv2; the README points to the author for other licensing. Replacing libgcc routines needs explicit calls to the qfp_* API.
caveats: README table only: GCC cycle counts are described as approximate averages; compiler version and flags for the GCC library are not stated, and no benchmark harness or C reference is in the visible repo listing. The 'GoFast' library column was not measured by the author but inferred from an ARM7TDMI page (author notes it may not be a fair comparison). This repo is a mirror packaged for RT-Thread; the original page quinapalus.com/qfplib.html was not opened (blogs blocked in this session). Last commit 2021.
found_via: Blogs / talks: WebSearch 'Cortex-M0 hand-written assembly floating point library faster than libgcc soft-float blog github routines cycles' (result snippet pointing to the Qfplib-M0-full README); README opened on github.com

name: zeebo/blake3 (Go BLAKE3 with avo-generated AVX-512, AVX2, SSE4.1, NEON assembly)
baseline: The same library built without its assembly (pure Go, compiled by the Go toolchain), plus the upstream Rust blake3 crate (single-threaded) shown in charts
workload: BLAKE3 hashing of 64 B to 1024 KiB inputs, full-buffer, incremental and reset modes; x86 on an i7-6700K (AVX2) and arm64 on an Apple M4 (NEON).
claimed_speedup: x86 full-buffer 1024 KiB: 262us vs 883us for the no-ASM build (derived from page data: about 3.4x; the README's own rate column lists 4.00GB/s vs 595MB/s, which does not match its timings). 1 KiB: 1.01us vs 1.77us (derived: about 1.75x). 64 B: 205ns vs 254ns. Apple M4 NEON, 1024 KiB: 459us (2.29GB/s) vs 1.00ms pure Go (1.05GB/s), about 2.2x (derived); at 1 KiB NEON and pure Go are equal (1.10us vs 1.08us). README says large inputs perform similarly to the Rust crate and small inputs are 3-4x slower in rate than Rust because of internal buffering.
compiler_and_flags: Go toolchain (version not stated), default flags; 'No ASM' tables come from building without the assembly
hardware: Intel i7-6700K (no AVX-512, so the AVX-512 kernels were not measured) and Apple M4; the author says CPU throttling and noise were not controlled
tradeoffs: Go only (not callable from C++ without cgo). Assembly is emitted by Go programs written with avo (the _asm directory), not hand-typed .s files. x86-64 with AVX2/AVX-512/SSE4.1 plus arm64 NEON/SVE2 variants; other targets fall back to pure Go. Does its own internal buffering and is single-threaded, so very small inputs are slower than the Rust crate. LICENSE file is CC0 and LICENSE-MIT is also present.
caveats: First-party numbers with an unstated Go version; author states no attempt at precise measurement. The 1024 KiB no-ASM row is internally inconsistent (880us at 596MB/s implies about 0.5 MiB), so the derived ratio uses timings only. The Rust comparison appears only as SVG charts, whose numbers were not read. The baseline is the same Go code without assembly, not a compiler -O3 build of a separate C function.
found_via: Blogs / talks: no blog result; found by checking Go repositories whose assembly is generated with avo (the avo project is described in blog posts) against the known list; README opened via raw.githubusercontent.com

name: lukechampine/blake3 (Go BLAKE3 with avo-generated AVX-512 and AVX2 assembly)
baseline: The same package's pure-Go implementation (Go compiler output)
workload: Go benchmarks BenchmarkSum256 (64 B, 1 KiB, 64 KiB), BenchmarkWrite and BenchmarkXOF, run with the AVX-512, AVX2 and pure-Go code paths.
claimed_speedup: Sum256 65536 B: 16245 ns (4034 MB/s) AVX-512, 31137 ns (2105 MB/s) AVX2, 133505 ns (491 MB/s) pure Go; ratios derived from page data: about 8.2x for AVX-512 and about 4.3x for AVX2. Write: 245 ns vs 2022 ns (about 8.3x). XOF: 246 ns vs 1914 ns (about 7.8x). No gain for 64 B and 1 KiB inputs (identical figures in all three listings).
hardware: README: '2020 MacBook Air (i5-7600K @ 3.80GHz)' (the label is internally inconsistent: that CPU is a desktop part without AVX-512)
tradeoffs: Go only. Assembly is generated by avo programs (avo directory), with all 7 rounds inlined, so the routines are thousands of lines. No assembly routine for single-block compressions, so inputs near 1 KiB gain nothing. Aims at eventual inclusion in x/crypto.
caveats: Author's own run: the Go version, flags and exact CPU are not stated or contradictory, and the identical 64 B and 1 KiB rows in the three blocks suggest the small-input rows were copied. Benchmark code is in blake3_test.go but was not opened. Baseline is the project's own pure-Go path, not a third-party library. The hardware line says the author expects better AVX-512 numbers on other machines.
